questions.stem: Memory cells of the human immune system — responsible for long-term immunity after infection — are a type of:
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes are a class of white blood cell (B-cells and T-cells). After an infection or vaccination, a subset of B-cells (memory B-cells) and T-cells (memory T-cells) persist for years, ready to respond rapidly if the same pathogen returns. This is the biological basis of vaccination and of 'natural immunity' after infection. Neutrophils are first-responder innate-immunity cells, not memory cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is NOT caused by a virus?
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis — bacterial, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. India carries the world's largest TB burden. Polio — viral (poliovirus, now near-eradicated globally thanks to OPV). Hepatitis B — viral (HBV, DNA virus). COVID-19 — viral (SARS-CoV-2, RNA virus). Common bacterial diseases — TB, typhoid, cholera, tetanus, plague, leprosy, pneumonia. Common viral — measles, mumps, rubella, flu, AIDS, rabies, dengue, chikungunya.

questions.stem: The mosquito species that transmits malaria is:
questions.explanation: The female Anopheles mosquito transmits malarial Plasmodium parasites. Only females bite — they need blood proteins for egg-laying. Male Anopheles feed on plant nectar. Culex mosquitoes transmit filariasis (lymphatic filariasis) and Japanese encephalitis. Aedes aegypti carries dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever. Mansonia also carries filariasis. Ronald Ross won the 1902 Nobel Prize for work in Secunderabad showing the mosquito-malaria link.

questions.stem: India's Universal Immunisation Programme currently protects against how many vaccine-preventable diseases?
questions.explanation: UIP, launched in 1985, currently provides free vaccines against 12 diseases: Tuberculosis, Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Polio, Hepatitis B, Measles, Rubella, Rotavirus diarrhoea, Pneumonia (Pneumococcal), Japanese Encephalitis (select states), Haemophilus Influenzae type B. Mission Indradhanush (2014) targets children and pregnant women not yet fully covered. India was certified polio-free in 2014.

questions.stem: Edward Jenner's pioneering vaccine (1796) was for:
questions.explanation: Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught the mild 'cowpox' virus were immune to the deadly smallpox — and tested this by inoculating a farm boy (James Phipps) with cowpox. 'Vaccine' — from Latin 'vacca' (cow). Smallpox became the first disease eradicated worldwide (declared 1980 by WHO). Pasteur's rabies vaccine came later (1885). BCG for TB (Calmette-Guérin, 1921). Salk polio vaccine — 1955.

questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is NOT transmitted through contaminated water?
questions.explanation: Influenza (flu) is an airborne respiratory virus, spread by droplets from coughs / sneezes / talking. Water-borne diseases — cholera (Vibrio cholerae), typhoid (Salmonella typhi), Hepatitis A and E (faeco-oral route), diarrhoea, amoebic dysentery, giardiasis — spread by drinking contaminated water. WASH (water, sanitation, hygiene) programmes target these. Airborne diseases need completely different control (masks, ventilation, vaccines).

questions.stem: The ABO blood-group system — that classifies people as A, B, AB or O — was discovered by:
questions.explanation: Karl Landsteiner (Austria, later USA) discovered the ABO blood-group system in 1900; won the 1930 Nobel Prize. Also discovered the Rh system (1940). Fleming discovered penicillin (1928); Pasteur pioneered vaccines and microbiology (pasteurisation); Mendel worked on pea-plant genetics (1860s). ABO compatibility — 'O negative' is the universal donor; 'AB positive' the universal recipient.
